papers.title_in_file: A quantum algorithm providing exponential speed increase for finding eigenvalues and eigenvectors
papers.version_note: The file is the arXiv preprint quant-ph/9807070v1 dated 24 Jul 1998 (the file name says 1999). The record names the Abrams and Lloyd eigenvalue paper, so the file matches. The PDF has no figures or tables; pdfimages lists only 1x1 inline stencil masks.
sections_read: Introduction (problem statement, conditions on the approximate eigenvector)
Real Hamiltonians, locality and the simulation of U(t)
Basis sets and the initial state
Atomic physics benchmark (boron estimate, qubit counts)
papers.what_it_is: A 1998 arXiv preprint (quant-ph/9807070) by Abrams and Lloyd giving a quantum FFT based algorithm for eigenvalues and eigenvectors of a Hamiltonian, with qubit-count estimates for atomic problems.

assertions.value: The authors describe a polynomial time quantum algorithm that uses the quantum fast Fourier transform to find eigenvalues and eigenvectors of a Hamiltonian operator.
quotes: We describe a new polynomial time quantum algorithm that uses the quantum fast fourier transform to find eigenvalues and eigenvectors of a Hamiltonian operator
assertions.certainty_reason: An author's claim or a result of one study, not settled beyond the paper.

assertions.value: The authors state the problem as follows: given the time-evolution operator U for a Hamiltonian H and an approximate eigenvector Va of U that can be generated in quantum polynomial time, find the true eigenvector V and true eigenvalue.
quotes: an approximate eigenvector Va of U (and thus of H) that can be generated in quantum polynomial time
Call the true eigenvector V and the true eigenvalue λv.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper defines its own problem here.

assertions.value: The authors state that if the overlap of the approximate eigenvector with the true one is not exponentially small, the true eigenvector and eigenvalue can be found in time proportional to the inverse of the squared overlap and the inverse of the desired accuracy.
quotes: If the state Va satisfies the property that | Va|V |2 is not exponentially small
then V and λv can be found in time proportional to 1/ | Va|V |2 and 1/ǫ, where ǫ is the desired accuracy.
assertions.certainty_reason: An author's claim or a result of one study, not settled beyond the paper.

assertions.value: The authors state that all known classical algorithms require an exponential amount of time for the cases the algorithm addresses, whereas the quantum algorithm scales as a polynomial in the number of particles and the desired accuracy.
quotes: the algorithm requires an amount of time which scales as a polynomial function of the number of particles and the desired accuracy
whereas all known classical algorithms require an exponential amount of time.
assertions.certainty_reason: An author's claim or a result of one study, not settled beyond the paper.

assertions.value: The authors state that when U has exponentially large dimension, which it typically does, there are no known classical algorithms that can find even the eigenvalues in polynomial time.
quotes: there are no known classical algorithms that can find even the
eigenvalues in polynomial time.
assertions.certainty_reason: An author's claim or a result of one study, not settled beyond the paper.

assertions.value: The authors state that for a system with discrete energy levels not exponentially close together near the ground state, a classically obtained state vector with expected energy below the first excited state by a non-exponentially small amount must contain a non-negligible ground-state component and could serve as the approximate state.
quotes: if it is possible to obtain classically any state vector with expected energy merely less than the first excited state (by a non-exponentially small amount)
then this state vector must contain a non-negligible component of the ground state
assertions.certainty_reason: An author's claim or a result of one study, not settled beyond the paper.

assertions.value: The authors state that where no classical guess with the needed overlap can be obtained, the state vector may often be generated by a quantum algorithm such as quantum simulated annealing.
quotes: it may often be the case that the state vector Va may be generated using a quantum algorithm, such as quantum simulated annealing.
assertions.certainty_reason: An author's claim or a result of one study, not settled beyond the paper.

assertions.value: The authors state that the algorithm applies to any U that can be implemented in quantum polynomial time, whether or not it represents the time evolution for a given Hamiltonian.
quotes: We will now describe an algorithm which applies to any U that can be implemented in quantum polynomial time, whether or not it represents the time evolution operator corresponding to a given Hamiltonian.
assertions.certainty_reason: An author's claim or a result of one study, not settled beyond the paper.

assertions.value: The authors cite reference [8] for the result that the time evolution operator of any local Hamiltonian can be implemented in polynomial time on a quantum computer.
quotes: (It was shown in [8] that the time evolution operator corresponding to any local Hamiltonian can be implemented in polynomial time on a quantum computer.)
assertions.certainty_reason: An author's claim or a result of one study, not settled beyond the paper.

assertions.value: The authors state that the first part of the algorithm was described independently by Cleve and coauthors in [12] to find eigenvalues, but not eigenvectors, of unitary operators.
quotes: This first part of the algorithm was described independently by Cleve et. al. in [12] to find eigenvalues (but not eigenvectors) of unitary operators
assertions.certainty_reason: An author's claim or a result of one study, not settled beyond the paper.

assertions.value: The authors set up a quantum computer of m+l+w qubits: m index qubits used for an FFT, l qubits for the Hilbert space in which U acts, and w working qubits for temporary storage. They state that the accuracy of the result grows as 1/M.
quotes: we consider a quantum computer consisting of m+l+w qubits
The accuracy of the result will grow as 1/M.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states its own register layout.

assertions.value: The authors describe building the state that holds U to the power j applied to Va, for each index j, by looping from 1 to M and applying U conditioned on a flag qubit that is set only while the loop count is less than j.
quotes: This transformation is accomplished by applying the operation U to the second set of l qubits (which are initially in the state |Va ) j times.
set a flag qubit to the value |1>if and only if i <j and perform the operation U conditioned on the value of this flag.
assertions.certainty_reason: An author's claim or a result of one study, not settled beyond the paper.

assertions.value: The authors state that, once the state is rewritten in the eigenbasis of U, a quantum FFT on the index qubits reveals the phases and thereby the eigenvalues.
quotes: It is now self-evident that a quantum FFT performed on the m index qubits
will reveal the phases ωk and thereby the eigenvalues λk.
assertions.certainty_reason: An author's claim or a result of one study, not settled beyond the paper.

assertions.value: The authors state that the quantum FFT requires only poly(m) operations, whereas the accuracy of the result scales linearly with M.
quotes: The quantum FFT requires only poly(m) operations, whereas the accuracy of the result will scale linearly with M or 2m.
assertions.certainty_reason: An author's claim or a result of one study, not settled beyond the paper.

assertions.value: The authors state that each frequency occurs with amplitude equal to the overlap of Va with that eigenvector, so measuring the index qubits yields each eigenvalue with probability equal to the squared magnitude of that overlap, and a polynomial number of trials suffices to obtain any eigenvalue whose overlap is not exponentially small.
quotes: by performing a measurement on the m index qubits, one thus obtains each eigenvalue with probability |ck|2.
Only a polynomial number of trials is therefore required to obtain any eigenvalue for which ck is not exponentially small.
assertions.certainty_reason: An author's claim or a result of one study, not settled beyond the paper.

assertions.value: The authors state that once an eigenvalue is measured, the remaining l qubits collapse into the state of the corresponding eigenvector, so the eigenvectors are obtained as well.
quotes: once a measurement is made and an eigenvalue λk is determined, the remaining l qubits “collapse” into the state of the corresponding eigenvector.
assertions.certainty_reason: An author's claim or a result of one study, not settled beyond the paper.

assertions.value: The authors state that the eigenvector remains trapped inside the computer because the phases of its amplitudes cannot be stored as classical information, but that properties such as charge density distributions, correlation functions and momentum distributions can be determined by measurements on the state.
quotes: since it is impossible to store as classical information the 2l phases associated with the state, one cannot possibly hope to do better.
easily obtainable properties include those of greatest interest: charge density distributions, correlation functions, momentum distributions, etc.
assertions.certainty_reason: An author's claim or a result of one study, not settled beyond the paper.

assertions.value: The authors state that the techniques apply to a different Hamiltonian, or one with additional terms, as long as it can be separated into a sum of local interactions, meaning terms that act on only k qubits with k independent of the number of particles n.
quotes: as long as the Hamiltonian can be separated into a sum of local interactions (that is, a sum of terms which act upon only k qubits, where k is independent of the number of particles n).
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states the scope of its method.

assertions.value: The authors state, citing the analysis in [8], that to simulate U(t) with accuracy epsilon one needs to apply order t squared over epsilon quantum logic operations.
quotes: A careful analysis [8] reveals that in order to simulate U (t) with an accuracy ǫ, one needs to apply O(t2/ǫ) quantum logic operations.
assertions.certainty_reason: An author's claim or a result of one study, not settled beyond the paper.

assertions.value: The authors state in a footnote that the number of quantum logic operations required to calculate the energy eigenstates to a precision epsilon scales as epsilon to the power minus two, because U must be calculated with greater precision when a shorter time t is chosen.
quotes: the number of quantum logic operations required to calculate the energy eigenstates to a precision ǫ is seen to scale as ǫ−2.
assertions.certainty_reason: An author's claim or a result of one study, not settled beyond the paper.

assertions.value: The authors state that in the usual first quantized representation each particle is described by l qubits holding a single particle wave function, so the system as a whole needs n*l qubits.
quotes: In the usual first quantized representation, each particle is described by a series of l qubits representing a single particle wave function.
The system as a whole is thus represented with n*l qubits.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states its own encoding.

assertions.value: The authors state, citing [6], that for a fixed-size single particle basis the operators Ui can always be calculated in the chosen basis and implemented using on the order of d to the fourth power operations, where d is the dimension of the single particle basis set.
quotes: the operators Ui can always be calculated in the chosen basis and implemented using O(d4) operations, where d is the dimension of the single particle basis set [6].
assertions.certainty_reason: An author's claim or a result of one study, not settled beyond the paper.

assertions.value: The authors state a trade-off between memory and speed: a position or momentum space representation needs only O(poly(log d)) operations per Ui but many qubits, while a more elaborate basis set reduces the qubits but may need a much larger number of operations per Ui.
quotes: there is a trade-off between memory and speed.
By choosing a more elaborate basis set, one can vastly reduce the required number of qubits, but a much larger number of quantum logic operations O(k4) may be necessary to implement each Ui.
assertions.certainty_reason: An author's claim or a result of one study, not settled beyond the paper.

assertions.value: The authors state that the initial state will normally be the result of a classical calculation such as a Hartree-Fock or configuration interaction calculation, and that techniques based on density functional theory are not usable because a wavefunction, not only a charge density distribution, is required.
quotes: Normally, the initial state Va will be the result of a classical calculation, for example, a Hartree-Fock calculation or configuration interaction calculation.
(Note that this does not include those techniques which utilize density functional theory, as we require a wavefunction, not simply a charge density distribution).
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states the input it requires.

assertions.value: The authors state that the quantum algorithm corresponds most closely to complete active configuration interaction or full configuration interaction, since the many-particle basis includes all possible products of single particle basis vectors, and that this approach is most valuable where the correlation energy is large and many configurations have similar energy.
quotes: The quantum algorithm corresponds most closely to what is known as “complete active configuration interaction” or “full configuration interaction” techniques
This approach is most valuable in situations where the correlation energy is large and where many “configurations” are of similar energy
assertions.certainty_reason: An author's claim or a result of one study, not settled beyond the paper.

assertions.value: The authors state that it is difficult to state precisely the minimum problem size for which the quantum calculation surpasses the best classical calculations, because sophisticated classical techniques avoid the exponential explosion in basis states.
quotes: Unfortunately, it is difficult to state precisely the minimum size problem for which the quantum calculation surpasses the best classical calculations
assertions.certainty_reason: An author's claim or a result of one study, not settled beyond the paper.

assertions.value: The authors estimate, based on a private communication [10], that an energy-level calculation of boron (5 electrons) with roughly 20 angular and 40 radial wavefunctions per particle, 800 single particle wave functions and a correspondingly huge full many-body basis, may give more accurate results than any classical calculation performed to date.
quotes: Based on [10], however, we estimate that a calculation of the energy levels of B (5 electrons), using roughly 20 angular wavefunctions and 40 radial wavefunctions per particle - for a total of 800 single particle wave functions and therefore 8005 ≈1015 full many-body basis states
may provide more accurate results than any classical calculation performed to date.
assertions.certainty_reason: An author's claim or a result of one study, not settled beyond the paper.

assertions.value: The authors state that a quantum calculation of the boron ground state with the described basis can be accomplished with 60 qubits: 10 per particle for a total of 50 qubits, 6 or 7 qubits for the FFT, and a few additional scratch qubits.
quotes: A quantum calculation of the B ground state, using a basis set as described above, can be accomplished with 60 qubits: 10 per particle to represent the state of the atom (for a total of 50 qubits), 6 or 7 qubits for the FFT, and a few additional “scratch” qubits3.
assertions.certainty_reason: An author's claim or a result of one study, not settled beyond the paper.

assertions.value: The authors state in a footnote that the accuracy scaling linearly with FFT size holds only for a fixed U, that increasing the evolution time t gives the eigenvalues to arbitrary precision with a fixed number of FFT points, and that the FFT must be large enough to separate the frequencies of distinct eigenvectors, which gives the estimate of 6 or 7 qubits (64 or 128 FFT points).
quotes: By changing U - in particular, by increasing the length of time t in U(t) - one can obtain the eigenvalues to arbitrary precision using a fixed number of FFT points.
This is how the estimate of 6 or 7 qubits (64 or 128 FFT points) is made.
assertions.certainty_reason: An author's claim or a result of one study, not settled beyond the paper.

assertions.value: The authors state that the two particle operators from the Coulomb attraction are represented by matrices with 240 elements (exponent flattened in the text layer), and that implementing such an operator by brute force is likely to remain intractable for the foreseeable future.
quotes: they therefore are represented by matrices with 240 elements.
Implementing such an operator by brute force is likely to remain intractable for the foreseeable future.

assertions.value: The authors estimate that 30 qubits per particle (10 per dimension, for a real space grid of 1024x1024x1024 per particle) will more than suffice for a position space representation, which makes the Coulomb terms easy to calculate but needs many more qubits.
quotes: We estimate that 30 qubits per particle (10 per dimension, for a real space grid of 1024x1024x1024 per particle) will more than suffice.

assertions.value: The authors state that the improved algorithm needs 2 x 30 qubits for the interacting particles, an additional 3 x 10 qubits for the remaining particles, and 10 qubits for the FFT and work space, and conclude that an interesting calculation needs a quantum computer with approximately 100 qubits.
quotes: the new efficient algorithm requires a total of 2 x 30 qubits (for the interacting particles), an additional 3 x 10 qubits (for the remaining particles), and the same 10 qubits for the FFT and work space.
one will need a quantum computer with approximately 100 qubits.

papers.what_it_is: The FOCS 2004 / SIAM J. Comput. paper by Aharonov, van Dam, Kempe, Landau, Lloyd and Regev proving that adiabatic quantum computation is polynomially equivalent to standard quantum computation, using 3-local Hamiltonians and 2-local nearest neighbor Hamiltonians on a two-dimensional grid of six-state particles.

assertions.value: The authors describe an efficient adiabatic simulation of any given quantum algorithm, which they state implies that the adiabatic computation model and the conventional quantum computation model are polynomially equivalent.
quotes: We describe an eﬃcient adiabatic simulation of any given quantum algorithm, which implies that the adiabatic computation model and the conventional quantum computation model are polynomially equivalent.
assertions.certainty_reason: An abstract summary; the theorem statements with conditions are entered separately.

assertions.value: The authors state that there is mounting evidence, citing [9, 10, 29], that the adiabatic algorithm of [14] takes exponential time in the worst case for NP-complete problems.
quotes: there is now mounting evidence [9, 10, 29] that the algorithm of [14] takes exponential time in the worst-case for NP-complete problems.
assertions.certainty_reason: A result the paper attributes to other work.

assertions.value: The authors state that several simulations on random instances of up to 20 quantum bits led to various optimistic speculations about the adiabatic algorithm of Farhi and coauthors.
quotes: several simulations (see, e.g., [13]) on random instances of up to 20 quantum bits led to various optimistic speculations.
assertions.certainty_reason: A result the paper attributes to other work.

assertions.value: The authors state that a small scale adiabatic algorithm has already been implemented experimentally on a Nuclear Magnetic Resonance system, citing [36].
quotes: We note that a small scale adiabatic algorithm has already been implemented experimentally, using a Nuclear Magnetic Resonance (NMR) system [36].
assertions.certainty_reason: A result the paper attributes to other work.

assertions.value: The authors state, citing [8], that adiabatic computation exhibits inherent robustness against certain types of quantum errors.
quotes: it exhibits inherent robustness against certain types of quantum errors [8].
assertions.certainty_reason: A result the paper attributes to other work.

assertions.value: The authors define the adiabatic model: a computation is specified by two local Hamiltonians Hinit and Hfinal, the ground state of Hinit is an easy to prepare state, the output is the ground state of Hfinal, and the running time is set by the minimal spectral gap along the straight line H(s) between them, polynomial if the gap is at least inverse polynomial.
quotes: A computation in this model is speciﬁed by two Hamiltonians named Hinit and Hﬁnal
The output of the adiabatic computation is the ground state of the ﬁnal Hamiltonian Hﬁnal.
More precisely, the adiabatic computation is polynomial time if this minimal spectral gap is at least inverse polynomial.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper defines or scopes its own setup here.

assertions.value: The authors state that it is known, citing [9, 13], that adiabatic computation can be efficiently simulated by standard quantum computers, so its computational power is not greater than that of standard quantum computers.
quotes: It is known that adiabatic computation can be eﬃciently simulated by standard quantum computers [9, 13].
assertions.certainty_reason: A result the paper attributes to other work.

assertions.value: The authors state that, per [9, 30], Grover's quadratic speed-up for unsorted search can be realized as an adiabatic computation.
quotes: In [9, 30] it was shown that Grover’s quadratic speed-up for an unsorted search [16] can be realized as an adiabatic computation.
assertions.certainty_reason: A result the paper attributes to other work.

assertions.value: The authors state that [11, 29, 32] showed adiabatic computation can tunnel through wide energy barriers and thus outperform simulated annealing, a classical counterpart of the adiabatic model.
quotes: [11,29,32] showed that adiabatic computation can ‘tunnel’ through wide energy barriers and thus outperform simulated annealing
assertions.certainty_reason: A result the paper attributes to other work.

assertions.value: The authors state that before this work it was not known whether adiabatic computation can achieve the full power of quantum computation, and not even whether it can simulate general classical computations efficiently.
quotes: However, whether adiabatic computation can achieve the full power of quantum computation was not known.
even the question of whether adiabatic computation can simulate general classical computations eﬃciently was unknown.
assertions.certainty_reason: An author's claim or a result of one study, not settled beyond the paper.

assertions.value: The authors state that they use adiabatic computation in the general sense in which the only restriction on Hfinal is that it is a local Hamiltonian, not the restricted adiabatic optimization algorithms in which Hfinal is diagonal, and that this definition is what allows them to prove their results.
quotes: we associate the term adiabatic computation with the more general class of adiabatic algorithms, where the only restriction on Hﬁnal is that it is a local Hamiltonian.
It is this natural deﬁnition that allows us to prove our results.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states the scope of its own model.

assertions.value: The paper states Theorem 1.1: the model of adiabatic computation is polynomially equivalent to the standard model of quantum computation. The authors state that the new direction, simulating standard quantum computation by adiabatic computation, uses adiabatic computation with 3-local Hamiltonians.
quotes: Theorem 1.1 The model of adiabatic computation is polynomially equivalent to the standard model of quantum computation.
We do this by using adiabatic computation with 3-local Hamiltonians.
assertions.certainty_reason: Stated as a theorem in Section 1.1 and proved in Sections 3 and 4.

assertions.value: The authors state that one direction of the equivalence, that adiabatic computation can be simulated by standard quantum computation, was already known from [13, 9], and that their contribution is the other direction.
quotes: As mentioned above, one direction of the equivalence is already known [13,9].
Our contribution is to show that standard quantum computation can be eﬃciently simulated by adiabatic computation.
assertions.certainty_reason: One direction is attributed to other work.

assertions.value: The authors define explicit sparse Hamiltonians as Hermitian matrices that have at most polynomially many nonzero elements in each row and column, for which an efficient Turing machine can generate a list of all nonzero entries in a given row or column.
quotes: These are Hermitian matrices that have at most polynomially many nonzero elements in each row and column
there is an eﬃcient Turing machine that can generate a list of all nonzero entries in a given row or column.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper defines or scopes its own setup here.

assertions.value: The paper states Corollary 1.2: the model of adiabatic computation with explicit sparse Hamiltonians is polynomially equivalent to the standard model of quantum computation. It rests on the authors' main theorem and on the result of [4] that adiabatic computation with explicit sparse Hamiltonians can still be simulated by standard quantum computation.
quotes: Corollary 1.2 The model of adiabatic computation with explicit sparse Hamiltonians is polynomially equivalent to the standard model of quantum computation.
It was shown in [4] that adiabatic computation with explicit sparse Hamiltonians can still be simulated by standard quantum computation
assertions.certainty_reason: Stated with its conditions; it follows from Theorem 1.1 and the cited result of [4].

assertions.value: The authors state that Theorem 1.1 uses 3-local Hamiltonians that act on particles that may be arbitrarily far apart, and that three-particle Hamiltonians are technologically very difficult to realize.
quotes: Theorem 1.1 uses 3-local Hamiltonians that act on particles that may be arbitrarily far apart.
three-particle Hamiltonians are technologically very diﬃcult to realize.
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors state this limit of their own theorem.

assertions.value: The paper states Theorem 1.3: any quantum computation can be efficiently simulated by an adiabatic computation with two-local nearest neighbor Hamiltonians operating on six-state particles set on a two dimensional grid.
quotes: Theorem 1.3 Any quantum computation can be eﬃciently simulated by an adiabatic computation with two-local nearest neighbor Hamiltonians operating on six-state particles set on a two dimensional grid.
assertions.certainty_reason: Stated as a theorem in Section 1.2 and proved as Theorem 4.1 in Section 4.

assertions.value: The authors state that the need for six-state particles arises from their construction and that it is an open question whether this can be improved.
quotes: The need for six-state particles arises from our construction. It is an open question whether this can be improved.
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors state this as left open.

assertions.value: The authors state that it remains to be further studied, both experimentally and theoretically, what the right model for noisy adiabatic computation is and whether fault tolerant adiabatic computation can be achieved.
quotes: it remains to be further studied, both experimentally and theoretically, what the right model for noisy adiabatic computation is, and whether fault tolerant adiabatic computation can be achieved.
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors state this as an open question.

assertions.value: The authors state the key observation of the construction: the ground state of Hfinal need not be the unknown final state of the circuit; it suffices, under some mild restrictions, that the ground state has a non-negligible inner product with it.
quotes: The key to resolve this diﬃculty is the observation that the ground state of Hﬁnal need not necessarily be the state |α(L) .
It is suﬃcient (under some mild restrictions) that the ground state has a non-negligible inner product with |α(L) .
assertions.certainty_reason: An overview of the approach; the formal statements are the later lemmas.

assertions.value: The authors state that they base their construction on Kitaev's result in [22], whose local Hamiltonian has as its ground state the entire history of the quantum computation in superposition, and that the Hamiltonian is Kitaev's, which gives the first quantum NP-complete problem.
quotes: Our idea is to base our solution on a seemingly unrelated ingenious result of Kitaev [22]
Kitaev’s local Hamiltonian has as its ground state the entire history of the quantum computation, in superposition
assertions.certainty_reason: A result the paper attributes to other work.

assertions.value: The authors state that the Hamiltonian used for the five-local construction involves five body interactions: three clock particles and two computation particles.
quotes: This Hamiltonian involves ﬁve body
